justice: Spatial resources are heavily allocated to motor vehicles: a wide paved carriageway with a centerline is present, while there is no clearly built sidewalk on either side (pedestrian space appears as dirt/grass shoulders).

Accessibility is limited by uneven roadside surfaces: the right side shows a narrow dirt verge with a drainage inlet/edge and exposed soil, which can be difficult for strollers, wheelchairs, and anyone needing a smooth continuous path.
Fairness across modes is weakened by missing dedicated facilities (no marked crossings, no cycle lane markings, no visible bus stop bay/shelter), making non-drivers depend on the roadway/shoulder.
safety: Pedestrian safety is reduced because there is no separated sidewalk; anyone walking likely shares space with vehicles on the pavement edge or the narrow dirt shoulder.
Cyclist safety is weak due to the absence of bike lanes or shoulder markings; the travel lane appears narrow with limited lateral buffer from passing vehicles.

Roadside encroachments and obstacles (wood piles/yard debris on the left, stacked materials near the right fence line) reduce clear recovery space and could increase crash severity or force pedestrians/cyclists closer to traffic.
livability: Low street activity and limited amenities are evident: the corridor is mostly walls/fences and vegetation with no visible shops, seating, or social spaces along the frontage.
The streetscape feels utilitarian and vehicle-oriented (long, straight roadway; sparse pedestrian infrastructure), which can discourage lingering or community interaction.
Environmental quality is mixed: while there is some greenery (large tree canopy on the right), the presence of debris/material piles and bare soil edges detracts from everyday pleasantness.
sustainability: Tree canopy and vegetation on the right side provide some ecosystem services (shade, potential air/dust mitigation), supporting environmental sustainability relative to fully hardscaped streets.
However, the corridor appears car-dependent due to the lack of safe walking/cycling infrastructure, which can push trips toward motorized travel.
Drainage appears conventional with a curbside inlet on the right, but there are no visible green stormwater features (e.g., bioswales/rain gardens) to support infiltration and runoff treatment.
aesthetics: The large mature tree on the right provides a strong natural visual element and helps frame the street.
Visual clutter from overhead utility wires and multiple poles weakens the streetscape’s visual order.
Untidy edges and stored materials (wood pile on the left; soil/mound and scattered items near the right) reduce perceived neatness and design quality.
comfort: Thermal comfort is uneven: the right side benefits from substantial tree shade, but most of the roadway and left side appear exposed with limited canopy.
Physical comfort for pedestrians is low because there is no paved sidewalk; walking would occur on uneven dirt/grass shoulders with surface discontinuities near drainage edges.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the lack of separation from moving traffic and the long, straight sightline that can encourage higher vehicle speeds, making walking/cycling feel stressful.
walkability: Sidewalk continuity is missing: neither side shows a constructed, continuous pedestrian walkway—only narrow, irregular shoulders.
Crossing support is absent: no marked crosswalks, curb ramps, or pedestrian refuge features are visible, limiting safe network connectivity for walkers.
Walking attractiveness is limited by few pedestrian-oriented elements (no benches, no street-level lighting designed for pedestrians, no clear wayfinding), and roadside debris reduces path usability.
bikeability: No dedicated cycling infrastructure is visible (no bike lane markings, no protected lane, no signed shared-lane treatment), forcing cyclists to mix with vehicle traffic.
The narrow/undefined shoulder space (dirt verge and edge drop to drainage on the right) provides poor operating space for cyclists and increases risk from passing vehicles.
No supporting end-of-trip features are visible (e.g., bicycle parking) and the corridor’s vehicle-oriented design reduces perceived cycling comfort and safety.
